Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 43, verse 5:

﴿Shall We then withhold the Reminder from you, turning away, because you are a people who exceed the limits?﴾ Meaning: shall We then turn aside from you the Reminder and drive it away from you, figuratively, from their saying: "he drove the strange camels away from the basin" (ḍarab al-gharā'ib ʿan al-ḥawḍ). From this is the saying of al-Ḥajjāj: "I will surely strike you the strike of strange camels." And Ṭarafa said:

"I strike away from you the worries that come upon you, / as you strike with the sword the forelock of the horse."

[[The explanation of this witness was given earlier in this volume, page 87, so refer to it if you wish. Its corrector.]]

The fa' here is for coordination with an omitted element, its sense being: "Shall We neglect you, so that We withhold the Reminder from you?", as a denial that the matter should be contrary to what was previously established of His sending down the Book and His making it an Arabic Qur'an, so that you might understand it and act by its requirements. Ṣafḥan (turning away) may be taken in two ways. Either it is a verbal noun from "ṣafaḥa ʿanhu" (he turned away from him), in the accusative as an object of purpose (mafʿūl lahu), meaning: "Shall We withdraw from you the sending down of the Qur'an and the imposition of proof by it, turning away from you?" Or it has the meaning of "side" from their saying: "he looked at him with the side of his face" (naẓara ilayhi biṣafḥi wajhihi wa ṣafḥi wajhihi), in the sense of: "Shall We remove it from you to one side?", so it is accusative as an adverb of place, as you say: "put it aside," and "walk aside." Supporting this is the reading of one who reads ṣufḥan with a ḍamma. In this reading there is another aspect: that it is a lightened form of ṣafūḥ, a plural of ṣafūḥ, and it is accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl), meaning: "turning away, averting."

Inna kuntum (in that you are): it means li-anna kuntum (because you are). It has also been read: in kuntum (if you are) and idh kuntum (since you are). If you ask: how does the sense of the conditional in (in) hold, when they were already excessive in their certainty? I answer: it is from the conditional that you mentioned, which is issued by one who is certain of the soundness of the matter, which is firmly established, as a hired worker says: "If I have worked for you, then pay me my due," while he knows this, but in his speech he gives the impression that your negligence in departing from the truth is the act of one who has doubt about entitlement, despite its clarity, to make him appear ignorant.

﴿And there came not to them﴾ is a *ḥikāyat ḥāl* (a narration of a past state that continues), meaning: they were in that condition. This is a consolation for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) regarding the mockery of his people. The pronoun in ﴿more severe than them﴾ refers to "the people who transgress," because the address was turned away from them toward the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), informing him about them. ﴿The example of the former peoples has passed on﴾ means: it has preceded in the Qur'an, in more than one place, the mention of their story and their wondrous condition, which deserves to become a proverb. This is a promise to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and a warning to them.

An example of this: you say to a man, "Who honoured you among the people?" and he says, "Zayd honoured me," and you say, describing the one mentioned: "The generous, the bountiful, whose attribute is such and such." Then, when the transition occurred from their speech to the speech of God, Mighty and Majestic, His speech proceeded according to what is known of iftinan (variety and artistry) in eloquence, so its beginning came in the third-person form and its end shifted from it to the first-person speaking in His saying ﴿then We revived﴾. All of that is variety among the branches of eloquence. Of this pattern is His saying, relating from Moses: ﴿He said: "Its knowledge is with my Lord in a Book; my Lord neither errs nor forgets. He began mentioning His attributes in the third-person form up to His saying ﴿We brought forth thereby pairs of various plants﴾. So look at the precise correspondence between the two verses and you will be amazed. And God is the Granter of success."]], then what will you make of His saying ﴿then We revived therewith a dead land; thus you will be brought forth﴾? And if it is from God's speech, what is its aspect?

I say: It is from God's speech, not from theirs. The meaning of ﴿Surely they will say: The Mighty, the Knowing created them﴾, with the attributes such and such, is: they will attribute the creation of them to the One whose attributes these are, and will ascribe it to Him. ﴿With a measure (bi-qadar)﴾: with a measure by which lands and servants are kept safe, and it was not a deluge.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 43, verses 15–18:

They have ascribed to Him, from among His servants, a part (juz'). This is connected to His words: ﴿And if you asked them, "Who created the heavens and the earth?" they would surely say, "God."﴾ That is, if you asked them about the Creator of the heavens and the earth, they would certainly acknowledge Him. Yet, along with that acknowledgment, they have ascribed to Him a share from among His servants, and so they described Him with the attributes of created beings. The meaning of ﴿a part from among His servants﴾ is that they said the angels are the daughters of God. They made them a part of Him and a portion of Him, just as a child is a piece of his father and a part of him.

Among the strange interpretations (bida' al-tafsir, i.e., innovated exegesis) is the explanation of juz' as "females," together with the claim that in the Arabic language juz' is a name for females. This is nothing but a lie against the Arabs, a fabricated and spurious invention. It did not satisfy them, so they derived from it the verb "ajza'at al-mar'a" (the woman gave birth to a female), and then they composed a line of verse:

*"If a free woman bears a female one day, it is no wonder; / the free woman who usually bears males may sometimes bear a female."*

It was said: "al-juz'" is a name for a female, and from it they derived "ajza'at al-mar'a," meaning when she gives birth to a juz', i.e., a female. Al-Zamakhshari rejected this and said it is a fabrication, not a genuine usage of the language. The meaning of the line is: if a free woman gives birth to a female at times, it is no wonder, for a free woman who usually bears males may sometimes bear a female. It was also said: "Hurrah" in the first (line) is a proper name of a woman, and the second is an adjective.

*"He married her from the daughters of al-Aws, one who gives birth to females, / for the pliant spindle-wood of al-'awsaj (a thorny shrub) has a whirring sound in its rotations."*

It was said: "al-mujazza'a" is the woman who bears daughters, and al-juz' is a daughter. Al-Zamakhshari rejected this and said: it is fabricated, not a genuine usage of the language. Al-'awsaj is a kind of thorn. What is meant by it is the spindle-stick made from it. Ladun means soft. Al-zajal is the sound of the spindle's rotation.

Its like is: *"wa-zawwajahā"* (and he married her), in the passive. It is also transmitted as *"nakahtahā min banāt al-Aws"* (I married her from the daughters of al-Aws). Al-Aws is the ancestor of a tribe named after him, and that woman bears daughters. He described the 'awsaj as pliant because of its greater humming and resonance when it turns.

It is also read *juz'an* with two damma (*juz'an*, with both letters vowelled). ﴿Surely man is an evident ingrate.﴾ That is, obvious ingratitude toward the blessing, whose ingratitude is clear, because ascribing offspring to Him is disbelief, and disbelief is the root of all ingratitude.

﴿Or has He taken daughters out of what He creates, and chosen sons for you?﴾ Here "am" means "rather" (bal), and the hamza is for denial and for making them look ignorant and an object of wonder at their state. For they were not content to ascribe a part to God from among His servants; they went so far as to make that part the worse of the two parts, namely females rather than males, even though they were the most averse of all God's creatures to females and the most hateful toward them. Their hatred reached the point that they buried them alive. It is as if it were said: Suppose that ascribing offspring to Him were permissible, as a hypothesis and an illustration; are you not ashamed of the injustice in the division? And of your claim that He preferred you to Himself by giving you the better of the two parts and leaving Himself the worse and lower of them?

[Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is as if it were said: suppose that ascribing offspring to Him is permissible as a hypothesis and illustration; are you not ashamed of the injustice in the division? And of the claim that He preferred you to Himself..." Ahmad (ibn al-Munayyir) said: We, the people of the Sunnah, say that everything happens by the will of God, Exalted is He, even misguidance and guidance, following the evidence of reason and affirming the explicit text, such as His words: ﴿He leads astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills.﴾ The verse of Surat al-Zukhruf does not increase this correct belief except by smoothing its path and confirming it correctly and firmly. So we say: if the disbeliever says, "Had God willed, I would not have disbelieved," this is a word of truth by which he intends falsehood. As to its being a word of truth, that is what we have established. As to his intending falsehood by it, the disbeliever's aim in this is to have a proof against God, supposing that God's willing the misguidance of whoever is misguided entails that He would not punish him for it, since he only did what His will required, just as the Qadariyya (those who affirm human power over action), the brothers of the idolaters, supposed. They associated partners with their Lord and believed that misguidance occurred by the will of creatures against the will of the Creator. Those who associated the angels (as partners) were higher in rank than these, because these associated their base selves with the dominion of their Lord, who is singular in lordship, Exalted is He. When what we have said is clear, God only refuted their statement because they supposed it to be a proof against God, so God refuted their argument, exposed their wish, and explained that their statement issued from false conjecture and pure guessing. He said: ﴿They have no knowledge of that; they only guess.﴾ (43:20). The sister of this verse, in conjunction with this one, has clarified this estimate, namely His words in Surat al-An'am: ﴿The idolaters will say, "Had God willed, we would not have associated, nor would our fathers, nor would we have prohibited anything." Likewise did those before them deny until they tasted Our might. Say: Do you have any knowledge that you can bring out for us? You follow only conjecture, and you are only guessing.﴾ (6:148). So God explained that what drove these people to deny the messengers and to associate others with God was their delusion that they had a proof against God by their saying: ﴿Had God willed, we would not have associated.﴾ So He likened their state in relying on this fantasy to the state of their forebears. Then He explained that it is a belief arising from a deceptive conjecture and a false imagination, so He said: ﴿You follow only conjecture, and you are only guessing.﴾ Then, when He had nullified their claim that they had any proof in their statement against God, He established God's conclusive proof against them by His words: ﴿So God's is the conclusive proof.﴾ (6:149). Then He made clear that the refutation of them lies only in their using that as an argument against God, not because the statement is false in itself. So He said: ﴿Had He willed, He would have guided you all.﴾ (6:149). This is the meaning of their words, "Had God willed, we would not have associated," in that the implication of "had" (law) is the impossibility of the guidance because of the impossibility of the will. So the last verse indicates that God did not will their guidance, but willed their misguidance. Had He willed their guidance, they would not have gone astray. This is the upright religion, the straight path, the shining light, and the clear method. What refutes the argument of these people, while holding the belief that God willed the occurrence of misguidance from them, is that God made for the servant a capacity and an ease for guidance and other acquired acts, until the acts issuing from him became the locus of obligation, because they are voluntary, and necessarily differentiated from compulsory accidents. This verse established the proof and clarified it for those whom God chose for correct beliefs. Since it is a subtle distinction, it did not settle into the minds of those with dense understanding. Therefore their understandings were scattered and their thoughts altered. One group, the Qadariyya, went to extremes and believed that the servant does whatever he wishes against the will of his Lord, while the Jabriyya (those who affirm compulsion) erred and believed that the servant has no power or choice at all, and that all acts issue from him by compulsion. As for the people of truth, God granted them a portion of His guidance and directed them to the middle path. So they pursued the paths of peace, and the guide of success was their leader, illuminated by the lights of reason which guide to the view that all created things are by God's power and will. It did not escape their understanding that some acts are within the servant's capacity, because they found the distinction between the voluntary and the compelled to be necessary. But that capacity accompanies the act without effecting it, and distinguishes between the necessary and the voluntary in the depiction. This is the verification, and God is the guardian of success.]

Then He said: ﴿Is it one who is brought up in ornaments and is not clear in dispute?﴾ That is, "Is it one who is raised in adornment and luxury?" As for the second: ﴿and when he is compelled to contend with opponents and argue with men, he is unclear, having no clarity or proof with which to argue against his adversary.﴾ This is because of the weakness of women's minds and their deficiency compared to the natural constitution of men. It is said: a woman seldom speaks, but when she wants to speak her proof, she speaks against herself.

In it: He made being raised in adornment and luxury one of the faults and blameworthy traits, and a trait of the mistresses of the curtained chambers. So a man must avoid that, shun it, keep himself far from it, and live as 'Umar, may God be pleased with him, said: *"Be rough and coarse, and live a hard life, and be like the (wild) Ma'add."* [Abu 'Ubayd related it in al-Gharib: Abu Bakr ibn 'Ayyash narrated to us from 'Asim ibn Abi al-'Ajdaj al-Asadi, from 'Umar, may God be pleased with him, that he said this, and he added: "and make the head two heads" (hadith), as a mawquf report. Ibn Hibban transmitted it from the path of Abu 'Uthman, who said: The letter of 'Umar came to us, mentioning a story in which this appears.] If he wishes to adorn himself, he adorns his inner self with the garment of piety.

It is read *yunsha'*, *yanshi'*, and *yunasha'*. The analogue of *munasha'a* in the sense of *insha'* (producing) is *mughalah* in the sense of *ighla'* (raising).

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 43, verse 19:

They have combined in their disbelief three disbeliefs. This is because they attributed offspring to God, and they attributed to Him the lower of the two kinds, and made them among the angels, who are the most honoured of God's servants with God, [[His saying "who are the most honoured of God's servants with God" is the view of the Mu'tazila. As for the People of the Sunna, some humans are more honoured in their sight than an angel. (ع)]] so they belittled them and held them in contempt.

It is also read: "servants of the Merciful" (ʿibād al-Raḥmān), "slaves of the Merciful" (ʿabīd al-Raḥmān), and "servant of the Merciful" (ʿabd al-Raḥmān). This is a metaphor for their nearness and special standing. "Inātan" and "anthan" are plurals of plural. The meaning of "jaʿalū" is "named," and they said that they are females. It is also read "ashahidū" and "āshahidū," with a fatha-marked hamza and a damma-marked hamza, and "ā ashahidū" with an alif between them. This is mockery of them, meaning that they say this without their saying being supported by knowledge, for God did not compel them to know it, nor did they arrive at it by reasoning, nor did they comprehend it through a report that necessitates knowledge. Nothing remains except that they witnessed their creation, and they report this witnessing. "Their testimony will be recorded" (sa-tuktabu shahādatuhum), the testimony by which they bore witness concerning the angels' femaleness, "and they will be questioned" (wa-yus'alūn). This is a threat.

It is also read "sa-yuktabu" and "sa-naktubu," with the yāʾ and the nūn. And "shahādatuhum" and "shahādātuhum." And "yusāʾalūn," on the pattern of "yufāʿilūn."

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 43, verse 20:

﴿And they say: "Had the Most Merciful willed, we would not have worshipped them."﴾ These are two further disbeliefs, added to the three previous disbeliefs: their worship of the angels besides God, and their claim that their worship was by the will of God, as their brethren the Mujbira (the Determinists, a term here meaning the People of the Sunnah) say. [[His saying "the Mujbira" means the People of the Sunnah, who said that He, exalted is He, wills evil as He wills good, because nothing occurs in His dominion except what He wills. But this does not entail compulsion (jabr) and does not negate the servant's choice, because the servant has an acquisition (kasb) in his acts, even though they are in reality created by Him, exalted is He. Compulsion would only follow if the servant had no role whatsoever in his acts, like a feather in the wind, as the true Mujbira said.

God censured that statement of the disbelievers only because they uttered it in mockery and obstinacy, not as affirmation and conviction. The proof of this is the consensus (ijma') of the earlier generations (Salaf) of the community that what God wills comes to be, and what He does not will does not come to be. (ع)]]. If you say: why do you reject the one who says that they uttered it in mockery? And if they had uttered it in earnest, they would have been believers? I reply: there is no proof that they uttered it in mockery, and claiming what has no proof is baseless. Moreover, God, exalted is He, has related this from them as a censure and as testimony to their disbelief: that they ascribed to Him a portion of His servants, that He took daughters and favoured them with sons, that they made the noble angels females, that they worshipped them, and that they said: "Had the Most Merciful willed, we would not have worshipped them." So if they had been uttering these statements in mockery, then the utterance of the reported words [[His saying: "then the utterance of the reported words... etc." is disallowed, and likewise what follows it. The Mu'tazilah said: He does not will evil, on the basis that will (irada) is command (amr), and this is disallowed. May God pardon the author of the book for his loose tongue against the People of the Sunnah, and for making them brethren of the disbelievers. (ع)]] which is, in their view, faith, would have been praised by them, since these are words of disbelief that they uttered in mockery. It would remain that they were in earnest, and all of them would share in being words of disbelief. If they say: "We make only this last one to be spoken in mockery, apart from what precedes it," then their only motive is to distort the Book of God, "which falsehood cannot approach from before it or from behind it" (﴿Which falsehood cannot approach from before it or from behind it﴾), in order to level their false doctrine.

Had this been a true word they uttered in mockery, the words of God, ﴿They have no knowledge of that; they only guess﴾, would have no meaning. For whoever says "There is no god but God" in mockery should be rebuked for his mockery and not be called a liar, because it is not permissible to call a speaker of the truth a liar, whether he speaks in earnest or in mockery.

If you say: what is your view of the one who interprets ﴿what they have concerning it of knowledge﴾ with their saying "the angels are God's daughters," so that ﴿they only guess﴾ refers to that saying and not to linking their worship to the will of God? I reply: it is the contrivance of a deceiver and the distortion of an arrogant person. Similar to it is His saying: ﴿Those who associated partners with God will say: "Had God willed, we would not have associated anything, nor would our fathers, nor would we have forbidden anything." Thus did those before them deny [the truth]﴾.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 43, verses 21–22:

The pronoun in "min qablihi" (from before it) refers to the Qur'an or to the Messenger. The meaning is: they attached the worship of other than God to the will of God:

"a saying they uttered without it being based on knowledge." Then He said: "Or have We given them a Book before this Book, in which We attributed disbelief and ugly deeds to Us, so that they gained knowledge of that through revelation, and so they hold fast to that Book and argue with it?"

"Rather, they have no proof to hold fast to except their saying: 'Indeed we found our fathers upon a community (ummah), following a religion (din).'" It is also read as "ala immatin" with a kasra. Both readings derive from "al-umm," which is intention (al-qasd). So "ummah" is the path that is aimed at (tuamm), i.e., intended, like the journey toward the destination traveled to. "Ummah" also means the way of life in which one who intends (al-amm, the one who sets out) lives. It has been said that it means "upon a blessing and a good state."

"Upon their traces they are guided" is the predicate of "inna" (indeed). Or the adverbial phrase is an attached complement (silah) of "muhtadun" (guided).

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 43, verse 26–28:

It is read "barā'" (براء), with the bā' vowelled with a fatḥa or a ḍamma, and "bari'" (بريء), so that "fa-bari'" (فبرىء) and "barā'" (براء) are like "karīm" and "kirām" [[His saying "like karīm and kirām" is in al-Ṣiḥāḥ. Al-kirām, with a ḍamma, is like al-karīm. (ʿA.)]]. "Barā'" is a verbal noun like "ẓimā'" (thirst), and therefore the singular, dual, plural, masculine and feminine are all alike in it. It is said: "We are free of you" (naḥnu al-barā'u minka), and "al-khalā'u minka" (we are clear of you).

As for ﴿the One who created me﴾ (illā alladhī faṭaranī), there are more than one possibility. It may be in the accusative, as an exception that is disjunct (istithnā' munqaṭiʿ), as if he said: "But the One who created me, He will surely guide me." It may also be in the genitive, as a substitute (badal) for what is governed by "min", as if he said: "Indeed I am free of what you worship, except the One who created me."

If you ask: how can you make it a substitute when it is not of the same kind as what they worship, for two reasons? The first is that the essence of God differs from all essences, so it differs from the essences of what they worship. The second is that God the Exalted is not worshipped among them, while the idols are worshipped. I say: they used to worship God alongside their idols.

It may also be that "illā" is a qualifier meaning "other than" (ghayr), with "mā" in "mā taʿbudūn" being qualified, its implied sense being: "Indeed I am free of gods that you worship other than the One who created me." This is like His saying, ﴿Had there been in them gods other than God, they would have been corrupted﴾ (law kāna fīhimā ālihatun illā Allāhu la-fasadatā).

If you ask: what is the meaning of His saying "sa-yahdīnī" (He will guide me), as a future with deferment? I say: once he said "fa-huwa yahdīnī" (He guides me), and once "fa-innahu sa-yahdīnī" (He will surely guide me). **Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 43, verses 33–35:**

*Li-buyutihim* (for their houses) is a *badal ishtimal* (a substitute in the sense of inclusion, i.e. a noun that is part of, or belongs to, the thing it replaces) for *li-man yakfuru* (for those who disbelieve). It is also permissible that both are like the two *lams* in your saying: "I gave him a garment for his shirt."

It was read: *suqfan*, with a fatha on the *sin* and a sukun on the *qaf*; and with a damma on the *sin* and a sukun on the *qaf*; and with a damma on both. It is the plural of *saqf*, like *rahn* and *rahun* and *rihan*. It is related from al-Farra': it is the plural of *suqayfa*, and *suqfan* with two fathas, as if it were a dialect form of *saqf* and *suqufan*, and *ma'arij* and *ma'arij*. The *ma'arij* are the plural of *mi'raj*, or a collective noun for *mi'raj*, which are the ascents to the upper levels. *Alayha yazharun* means: upon the *ma'arij* they ascend. "They ascend the roofs" means they climb onto them, "so they were not able to ascend it."

*Wa-surura* was read with a fatha on the *ra'*, because of the heaviness of the two dammas together with the doubled letters.

*Lamma mata'u al-hayat*: the *lam* is the one that distinguishes the *inna* of lightened form (*mukhaffafa*) from the negating *inna*. It was read with a kasra on the *lam*, meaning: "that which is the enjoyment of the life," like His saying: ﴿a parable, even a gnat or anything above it﴾ (2:26). *Lamma*, with a doubled *mim*, is in the sense of *illa* (except), and *inna* is negating. It was also read *illa*, and it was read: *wa-ma kullu dhalika illa*.

When He said: ﴿better than what they accumulate﴾ (43:32), and belittled the affair of this world and made it small, He followed it with what confirms the insignificance of the world in His sight, in His saying: ﴿And were it not that mankind would be one community﴾ (43:33). That is: were it not that He disliked that they would gather together upon disbelief and unite upon it, He would have made for the weakness of the splendour of the life of this world:

[[Mahmud said: "Its meaning: were it not for the dislike that they would gather upon disbelief, He would have made for the disbelievers roofs of silver, that is, He would have extended the world for them, because of its insignificance in Our sight." Ahmad said: "'Were it not' (*lawla*) here is a sister of 'were it not' in His saying: ﴿And were it not that a disaster should afflict them for what their hands have sent forth …﴾ (28:47), and the rest of the verse. That is what corrects the statement by estimating the dislike of that, without supposing an omitted element as I mentioned before. So the sense of the statement here is that their unanimity upon disbelief is an impediment to the expansion of the world. This is the constant meaning of *lawla*: what follows it is always an impediment to its answer. But the impediment may actually exist, so the answer is clearly prevented, as in His saying: ﴿So were it not for the grace of Allah upon you and His mercy, you would have been among the losers﴾ (2:64), and this is the most common usage. It may also exist by estimation, together with it, and the verse is of this type: that is, if the expansion of the world for the disbeliever were to exist by estimation, its impediment would exist in Our sight, namely the gathering upon disbelief, existing by estimation with it. Everything whose existence leads to the existence of its impediment does not exist."]]

Among Us, for the disbelievers, would be roofs and ascents and doors and couches, all of silver and ornament, and We would make for them ornament (*zukhrufan*), that is, adornment, of every kind. *Al-zukhruf* means adornment and gold.

It is permissible that the original was: *saqfan min fiddatin wa-zukhrufan*, meaning: some of them of silver and some of them of gold, and so it is in the accusative as a coordinated element on the position of *min fiddatin*. In its meaning is the saying of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "If the world were weighed before Allah as much as the wing of a gnat, He would not give a disbeliever a sip of water from it."

[[In its chain is Abd al-Hamid ibn Sulayman, and Zakariya ibn Mandhur followed him. al-Tirmidhi said: "On this topic there is also a report from Abu Hurayra, and his hadith is in al-Bazzar through the narration of Salih, the client of al-Tawama, from him, and its wording is: 'He has not given a disbeliever anything of it.'" It is narrated by al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab in the seventy-first, through the narration of Abu Ma'shar from al-Maqburi, from him. And on this topic there is also a report from Ibn Abbas, which Abu Nu'aym recorded in al-Hilya. In it is al-Hasan ibn Ammara, who is very weak. It is recorded by al-Qada'i in Musnad al-Shihab through the narration of Malik from Nafi' from Ibn Umar, with the wording of the author. Ibn Tahir said: "In it is Ali ibn Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Abi Awf from Abu Mus'ab from him; it has no basis from the hadith of Malik."]]

If you say: since the disbelievers were not given expansion because of the trial that expansion upon them would lead to, namely the gathering of people upon disbelief through their love of the world and their eagerness for it, then why not expand upon the Muslims so that people would gather upon Islam?

I say: expansion upon them is also a corruption, since it leads to entering Islam for the sake of the world, and entering the religion for the sake of the world is the religion of the hypocrites.

[[Mahmud said: "Since He did not expand upon the disbelievers, because of the trial that expansion would lead to, namely the gathering upon disbelief …" Then: "Why not expand upon the Muslims so that people would gather upon faith?" And he answered that expansion upon them is also a corruption, since it leads to entering Islam for the sake of the world, and that is the religion of the hypocrites." Ahmad said: The question and answer are built upon two corrupt principles. One is the attributing of causes (*ta'lil*) to the actions of God, the Exalted; the other is that God, the Exalted, wills Islam from all creatures. As for the first, God silenced the questioner about it by His saying: ﴿He is not asked about what He does, but they will be asked﴾ (21:23). As for the second, God has sufficed the believers in answering it by His saying: ﴿And if your Lord had willed, all those on earth would have believed, all of them together﴾ (10:99).]]

So the wisdom in what He arranged was this: He made among both groups the rich and the poor, and poverty prevailed over wealth.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 43, verse 36–39:

It is read "wa man ya'shu" with the shin both damma-d and fatha-d. The difference between them is that when there is an affliction in his sight it is said 'ashiya (ʿashiya), and when he looks with the look of one who is ʿashī (ʿashī, weak-sighted) while having no affliction, it is said ʿashā. Its counterpart is ʿaraja (ʿaraja), used of one who has the affliction [[Mahmud said: "It is said ʿashiya his sight, with the shin kasra, when an affliction befalls it ..." Ahmad said: In this verse there are two wonderful subtleties. The first: the indication that an indefinite noun falling within the context of a conditional (sharṭ) conveys generality. This is a question on which the usulis (uṣūliyyūn, scholars of legal theory) have disagreed, and Imam al-Haramayn is among those who hold that it conveys generality, to the extent that he corrected the Imams for their absolute statement that an indefinite noun in an affirmative context is particularizing, and said: the conditional generalizes, and the indefinite noun within its scope generalizes. The jurist Abu al-Hasan al-Anbari, commentator on his book, refuted him vigorously. In this verse there is sufficiency for the Imam and for whoever holds his view, because the Shaytan is mentioned in it as an indefinite noun within a conditional context, and we know that it is only intended to mean the generality of shayatin, not a single one, for two reasons. One: it is established that every person has a shaytan, so how much more so for one who is blind to the remembrance of God. The other is derived from the verse: that it refers back to it with a plural pronoun in His saying "wa innahum", for it refers to the shaytan unanimously. "Were it not that it conveys the generality of inclusion, it would not be permissible to return a plural pronoun to it without difficulty." This is a subtlety that, when heard by opponents of this view, leaves them silent. The second subtlety: in this verse there is a refutation of those who claim that the return (of pronouns) must follow the meaning (ma'na) and forbids returning to its wording (lafz) afterwards. The one who forbids this argues that it is an ijmal (summary) after a tafsil (detail), which is contrary to the known eloquence.

Al-Kindi refuted this with the saying of the Exalted: "And whoever believes in God and does righteous deeds, He will admit him into gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever; God has indeed made good provision for him" (65:11). Others refuted it with His saying: "And among the people is he who purchases idle talk to mislead from the way of God without knowledge and takes it in ridicule; for them is a humiliating punishment. And when Our verses are recited to him ..." (31:6–7). My grandfather, may God have mercy on him, derived some of this from this verse, because he returned to the wording in His saying "yaʿshu" and "lahu" twice, then to the meaning in His saying "la-yaṣuddunahum", then to the wording again with "ḥattā idha jā'anā". I have already mentioned that whoever prohibits this may have restricted his prohibition to its occurrence in a single sentence; but when sentences are multiple and each stands independently, this may not be prohibited. I have already responded to al-Zamakhshari in his saying: "Who possess no intercession except he who has taken a covenant with the Most Merciful" (19:87), because it is a single sentence; look at it in its place.]].

And "ʿaraja" is used of one who walks with the gait of a lame man without being lame. Al-Hutay'a said:

"Whenever you come to him, looking toward the light of his fire [[He is a generous giver and a squanderer: when you ask him, he brightens and quivers like the quivering of an Indian sword.

And that man, if he gives you today with both his hands a gift, he does not withhold you from a gift tomorrow.

Whenever you come to him, looking toward the light of his fire, you find the best fire there, the best hearth.]]"

By Al-Hutay'a. He says: he is abundant in acquiring and abundant in squandering, and between them is the antithesis of opposites: when you ask him, he answers quickly and with a radiant face, and this is what is meant by "he brightens and quivers, like the quivering of a sword drawn from Indian iron"; if he gives you today a gift with both his hands together, a metaphor for abundance of giving, and you ask him tomorrow, he gives you again. "ʿashiya yaʿshā" like "riḍiya yarḍā": when there is an affliction in his sight. "ʿashā yaʿshū": when he feigns weak-sightedness without any affliction. The meaning: "Whenever you come to him in the state of one who is weak-sighted" — a metaphor for displaying need — "you find him the most generous of people," expressed thus by way of metonymy.

That is: you look at it with the look of one who is weak-sighted, because the abundance of fuel and the spreading of light weakens your sight. This is clear in the saying of Hatim:

"I feign blindness when my neighbour appears, until the curtain conceals my neighbour [[My fire and my neighbour's fire are one, and to it before me the cooking-pot descends.

No harm has come to me from a neighbour whom I host, that his door should lack a curtain.

I feign blindness when my neighbour appears, until the curtain conceals my neighbour.]]"

By Hatim al-Ta'i. "ʿashiya yaʿshā" like "riḍiya yarḍā": he became unable to see at night; "ʿashā yaʿshū" like "daʿā yadʿū": when he looked like one who is weak-sighted.

He says: my fire is the fire of my neighbour, and my cooking-pot descends to him to eat from it before me; or my fire and my neighbour's fire are one in time and strength, and yet his pot descends to him before mine, so that he eats it quickly for fear that someone will see him. But this is far-fetched, since the context is not dispraise of the neighbour but praise. Then this is a metonymy for the intensity of his generosity toward others. Then he describes himself as chaste by his saying: "No harm has come to me from any of my neighbours through reproach or otherwise, from his door lacking a curtain that screens his household, for I feign unawareness and lower my gaze when my neighbour goes out, until she is screened by her own." He used the apparent noun in place of the pronoun to indicate that the right of neighbourhood must be observed. The first possibility is more fitting, because its meaning is that he is kind to him and abstains from his womenfolk. As for the second, it involves dispraise of the neighbour, which does not suit what follows it.

And it is read "yaʿshū", taking "man" as a relative pronoun, not implying the meaning of a conditional. The one who reads thus should have the verb in the nominative ("yarfaʿ naqīḍ")... The meaning of the reading with fatha: "whoever is blind to the remembrance of the Most Merciful, which is the Qur'an," like His saying: "deaf, dumb, blind" (2:18). As for the reading with damma, its meaning is: "whoever feigns blindness to His remembrance," i.e., he recognises that it is the truth but pretends ignorance and feigns unawareness, like His saying: "And they denied them, though their souls were convinced of them" (27:14).

"We appoint for him a shaytan" — we leave him to his own devices [[His saying "We appoint for him a shaytan: we leave him to his own devices" is an interpretation based on the principle that He does not do what is ugly, which is the doctrine of the Mu'tazila. According to the Ahl al-Sunna, He is the creator of all existents, so the verses are upon their apparent meaning (ʿ).]] and leave him between himself and the shayatin, like His saying: "And We appointed for them companions" (41:25), "Have you not seen that We sent the shayatin upon the disbelievers" (19:83). It is also read "yuqayyid" (yuqayyiḍ), meaning: the Merciful appoints for him and the Shaytan appoints for him.

If you say: why is the pronoun of "man" pluralised, and the pronoun of the shaytan in His saying "wa innahum la-yaṣuddunahum"? I say: because "man" is indefinite regarding the class of the one who is blind, and a shaytan has been appointed for him, indefinite regarding his class. Since both may apply to more than one because of their indefiniteness, it is permissible for the pronoun to return to both in the plural. "Until, when he comes to Us" — the one who is blind. It is also read "jā'ānā" (jā'ānā), meaning the verb belongs to him and to his shaytan. He says: "O would that between me and you were the distance of the two easts" (43:38), meaning the east and the west, and he gave precedence to the one. As is said: "the two ʿUmars" and "the two Qamars." If you say: what is "the distance of the two easts"? I say: their remoteness; the original is "the distance of the east from the west and the west from the east." When one is given precedence and the two separated things are joined by the dual, the distance is attributed to both.

"That you" is in the place of nominative as the agent. The meaning: your sharing in the punishment will not benefit you, as the sharing of those who fall into a hard matter benefits them, because they help one another to bear its burdens and divide its severity and hardship; for each of you has a punishment beyond his capacity to bear. You may also take the verb as expressing a wish in His saying: "O would that between me and you were the distance of the two easts," meaning: what you are in of wishing to be far from your companion will not benefit you today. His saying "that you are in the punishment sharing" is a causal clause: your wish will not benefit you, because your due is that you and your companions share in the punishment just as you shared in its cause, which is disbelief. The reading of one who reads "innakum" with kasra strengthens this. It was said: when the one afflicted with severe hardship sees one who is afflicted with a like one, it eases him and relieves some of his distress, and this is the consolation that al-Khansa mentioned: "I console my soul for him with consolation."

"It will not console them, their sharing, nor ease them, because of the greatness of what they are in." — And His saying: "when you did wrong" — what is its meaning? I say: its meaning is: when your wrongdoing is established and made manifest, and neither you nor anyone has any doubt that you were wrongdoers; and that is the Day of Resurrection. "Idh" is a substitute for "the day." Its counterpart is:

"When we claim descent, a base woman did not bear me [[The explanation of this witness has passed in the third part, page 40, so refer to it if you wish. — its editor.]]"

That is: it became clear that I am the son of a noble woman.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 43, verse 46–47:

What they answered him with, at His saying ﴿Indeed, I am a messenger of the Lord of the worlds﴾, is omitted, and it is indicated by His saying ﴿So when he came to them with Our signs﴾, which is their demand that he bring evidence for his claim and display a sign. ﴿Behold, they laughed at them﴾: that is, they mocked them, made fun of them, and called them sorcery. Here "idha" (idha al-mufajaah, the "sudden" idha) denotes suddenness. If you say: how is it permissible for "lamma" (lamma, "when") to be answered by "idha" al-mufajaah? I say: because the verb of suddenness is implied with it, and it is the governing element of the accusative case [[Mahmud said: "It is permissible in it to have "lamma" answered by "idha" which is of suddenness, because the verb of suddenness is implied with it, and it is the governing element of the accusative case in it ... etc." Ahmad said: The apparent reason for permitting this usage, and God knows best, is that each one of these verses, when you consider it alone in thought, its greatness overwhelms the thought and dazzles it, until one is certain that it is the ultimate, and that every verse other than it is lesser. Then when the thought is shifted to its sister verse, it too fills the mind with its greatness, and it forgets the first and is certain that this one is the ultimate, and every verse other than it is lesser. The conclusion is that thought is not able to bring together two of these verses so as to establish with certainty which is superior and which is inferior; rather, whenever it considers one alone, it is certain that it is the ultimate. On this basis all similar cases that occur are to be understood, and God knows best.]] in its place, as if it were said: when He came to them with Our signs, they suddenly, at the time of their laughter, [were confronted].

**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 43, verse 48:**

If you say: when one sign from among the nine came to them, what is the sign that was said to surpass it in magnitude among the remaining signs? I say: its counterpart is a sign like it. This is the description of each one of them. So the meaning is that each is greater than the rest of the signs, by way of detailed examination and inductive survey, one after another, as you say: "He is the best man I have seen," meaning: his excellence over the whole body of men whom you have seen, when you go through them (qaraituhum) man by man. [[His saying "qaraituhum rajulan rajulan" means: I followed them up (tatabba'tuhum).]] If you say: this is contradictory, for its meaning is: there is no sign among the nine that is not greater than each one of them, so one of them would be both superior and inferior in one state. I say: the purpose of this statement is that they are all described as great, and they hardly differ in it. Likewise it is the custom with things that are alike in excellence but whose ranks differ only slightly, that people's opinions diverge on preferring them, so some prefer this and others that. On this basis people have framed their speech, saying: "I saw men, some of them better than others," and sometimes the opinions of a single man differ about them, so at one time he prefers this and at another time that. From this is the verse of the Hamasa (anthology):

Whomever you meet among them, you will have met their chief,
like the stars by which the night traveler is guided.

It is by 'Ubayd ibn al-Abras. It is also said to be by al-'Arandas. *Hayyinun layyinun* are plural of *hayyin* and *layyin*, a diminutive form of *hayyin* and *layyin* with tashdid, on the pattern *fay'il*.

*Aysar* is plural of *yusr*, as *qutb* and *aqtab*; it is originally the opposite of hardship (*'usr*), and a man was named with it as an intensification; or it is the plural of *yusra*, as *qasaba* and *qasaba*, which is originally the line in the inner part of the palm, and it was applied to a man to signal generosity. *Sawwas* is the plural of *sa'is*, meaning one who owns and manages with regard to welfare, and also the guardian who sets things right. *Jahada* the food means: he longed for it and desired it. *Jahada al-rajul* (the man), so he is *majhud*: he was struck by famine and hardship. His saying "fa-al-jahd yakhruju minhum" is the answer to the condition, and it is possible that it is a resumed construction (istinaf mufarragh) following what came before.

*Wa-in jahadu*: its answer is indicated by what precedes it. *Al-shahama* is roughness, and *shahamtu al-faras* means I moved it so that it would speed up. *Adhmar shurr* means: brave fighters of war, plural of *dhimr* as *kabid*, from *dhamara al-rajul*: he frowned and became angry; and *dhamara al-asad* means he roared with his voice; that is, if you urge them to war, you will reveal from them brave warriors who are not evil. The verb "yanturun" is construed with the sense of informing, so it takes *'an*. It is also permissible that it means *ba'*.

*Al-mumara'a* is disputation. *Bi-ikthar* is connected to *mara* or to *yumarun*.

Whomever you meet among them, you will meet their noblest, because they are equal in nobility; they are like the stars in their equality in nobility and in being guided by and illuminated by each of them. Just as the traveler is guided by a star, so they are guided by the one who seeks benevolence who is confused, or the one who is perplexed in a difficult matter. It is narrated instead of "wa-in jahadu ... ilakh":

... and if they are tested in hardship, the good report of them is attained,

that is: if they are tested, the knowledge of their generosity and good conduct is established.

The Anmariyya (mother of the Anmar) preferred among her perfect sons, then she said, having seen that their ranks were close and their difference slight:

May they be bereaved (*thakiltuhum*) [[His saying "thakiltuhum": *al-thakl* is a woman's loss of her child. (ʿ)]]. If I knew which of them is better, they are like a hollow ring, one does not know where its ends are.

﴿Perhaps they will return﴾, meaning the intention that they should turn back from disbelief to faith. [[He said: "its meaning is the intention that they should turn back from disbelief to faith, etc." Ahmad said: It has been established in more than one place that *la'alla*, wherever it occurs in the speech of Allah the Exalted, the intention is to direct the hope to the created beings, that is: so that they would be in a state in which such a thing is hoped for from them. This is the truth, and Sibawayh interpreted what occurred in this way. As for al-Zamakhshari, he takes *la'alla* to mean willing, because he does not shy away from the belief that God wills something while the servant wills its opposite, so the servant's will takes place and the Lord's will does not take place, may Allah be exalted far above what the wrongdoers say. How atrocious is this slip and how abominable this inclination! He has behaved badly at this point, to the extent that, were it not necessary to refute him, the pen would not have moved to transmit what he raved and what he was not guided to. He has followed the ways of his predecessors in making the reality of the command to be the will, and added to that the belief that the servant produces his act and creates it, and that the servant's will takes place while the Lord's will does not take place. These are three darknesses, one upon another; we seek refuge in Allah from this error: ﴿Our Lord, do not let our hearts deviate after You have guided us﴾.]]

If you say: if He willed their return, it would happen. I say: His willing the act of another is nothing but that He commands him to it and asks him to bring it into existence. If that is by way of compulsion, it occurs; otherwise it lies between its occurrence and its non-occurrence according to the choice of the accountable person. The return did not happen only because the will was not compulsion and they did not choose it. [[His saying "nothing but that He commands him to it" is the doctrine of the Mu'tazila. As for the doctrine of the people of the Sunna: His willing is other than commanding, whether it is for His own act or for the act of another, and it is not necessary to interpret the verse by will, since it is possible that its meaning is: so that their state, at the taking of the punishment, is the state of one who hopes for their return. (ʿ)]]

The punishment here means: the years of drought, the flood, the locusts, and other things.

Also recited: "Yā ayyuhā l-sāḥir" with the hā' vowelled with a ḍamma, and its reasoning has already been mentioned. If you ask: how did they call him "the sorcerer" while saying "Indeed, we are truly guided" (innā la-muhtadūn)? I answer: their saying "Indeed, we are truly guided" is a promise whose breaking was intended, a covenant firmly resolved to be broken, conditional upon his supplicating for them and the punishment being lifted from them. Do you not see the words of the Exalted: "But when We removed the punishment from them, behold, they broke their word" (fa-lammā kashafnā ʿanhumu l-ʿadhāba idhā hum yankuthūn)? So their calling him "the sorcerer" does not contradict their saying "Indeed, we are truly guided." It has also been said: they used to call the learned, skilled man "sāḥir" (sorcerer) out of their awe of magic.

"By what He has covenanted with you" (bimā ʿahida ʿindak): by His covenant with you, that your supplication is answered; or by His covenant with you, which is prophethood; or by what is covenanted with you, so that you fulfil it, which is faith and obedience; or by what is covenanted with you of the removal of punishment from those who are guided.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 43, verses 51–53:

﴿And Pharaoh proclaimed among his people﴾: he made them the place of his proclamation and the object of it. The meaning is that he ordered the proclamation to be made in their gatherings, and he attributed the proclaiming to himself, although it was someone else who proclaimed it in those places on his behalf. This is like your saying, "The amir cut off the thief's hand," when he ordered it to be cut off. It is also possible that the great men of the Copts were with him, so he raised his voice with it among them, and then it spread from him among the masses of the Copts, so it was as if it had been proclaimed among them. He said, ﴿Is not the dominion of Egypt mine, and these rivers flowing beneath me?﴾ meaning the rivers of the Nile, the principal of which are four: the Nahr al-Malik, the Nahr Tulun, the Nahr Damietta, and the Nahr Tinnis. It was said: they flowed beneath his palace. It was said: beneath his throne, because of its height. It was said: "before me," in my gardens and orchards.

It is also possible that the waw is conjunctive, joining "the rivers" to "the dominion of Egypt," and "flowing" is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to them. It is also possible that the waw is a waw of circumstance, the demonstrative is the subject (mubtada'), "the rivers" is an attribute of the demonstrative, and "flowing" is the predicate of the subject. I wonder how the aspiration to the claim of lordship rose in one who magnified himself by the dominion of Egypt, and how people marvelled at the extent of his greatness. He ordered it to be proclaimed in the markets and alleys of Egypt, so that that splendour and majesty would not be hidden from small or great, and so that the measure of his might and dominion would settle in the hearts of the common folk [[The editorial note in the text: "His saying 'that splendour' (tilka al-ubba) like sukra, so it is in the margin of the Sihah. And in the Sihah: 'dahmā' al-nās': their assembly. (ʿ)]].

It is reported from al-Rashid that when he read it he said, "I will certainly appoint to it the lowliest of my slaves," and he appointed al-Khasib, who used to be in charge of his ablutions. It is also reported from Abd Allah ibn Tahir that he was appointed to it, and when he set out toward it and it came into his view, he said, "Is this the city in which Pharaoh boasted, until he said, 'Is not the dominion of Egypt mine?' By God, it is less in my estimation than that I should enter it," and he turned his reins back.

﴿Or am I better than this one who is contemptible﴾: this is a connecting (muttaṣila) interrogative, because the meaning is "Will you not see, or will you see?" except that he placed his saying "am I better" in the position of "will you see," because when they said to him, "You are better," they were, in his view, perceptive. This is the placing of the cause in the position of the effect. It is also possible that it is a disconnected (munqaṭiʿa) one, meaning "Rather, am I better?" and the hamza is for affirmation. That is because it was a list enumerating the causes of excellence and precedence over them: the dominion of Egypt, the flowing of the rivers beneath him. He proclaimed that and filled their ears with it, then he said, "I am better," as if he were saying, "Let it be established and settled with you that I am better, and this is my state," ﴿than this one who is contemptible﴾, that is, weak and despicable. It was recited as ﴿amā anā khayr﴾ (a variant reading). ﴿And who can hardly express himself clearly﴾: the speech is because of the impediment in it (al-rutba), with a ḍamma, meaning the non-Arabic quality in speech, as in the Sihah. He means that he did not have with him the number and the instruments of rule and government by which he could be supported, and that in himself he was deficient in what men are described by in eloquence and fluency. All the prophets were clear (abyāʾ) and eloquent [[The editorial note in the text: "And the prophets were all abyāʾ": in the Sihah: bāna al-shayʾ bayānan: it became manifest, so it is bayyin, and its plural is abyāʾ, like hayyin and ahyāʾ. (ʿ)]].

By his casting of bracelets upon him he meant the conferring upon him of the reins of kingship, because when they wished to make a man a lord, they would put a bracelet on his wrist and a gold collar around his neck. ﴿Accompanied﴾: either "accompanied by him," from your saying "I conjoined him, so he was conjoined to him," or from "they accompanied one another," meaning they came together. When he described himself with dominion and might and compared himself with Moses, peace and blessings of God be upon him, and described him with weakness and few supporters, he raised an objection and said, "Why, if he is truthful, has his Lord not given him dominion, made him a lord, and placed bracelets on him, and made the angels his helpers and supporters?"

It was recited ﴿asāwir﴾, the plural of ﴿aswira﴾, and ﴿asāwīr﴾, the plural of ﴿siwār﴾, which is the bracelet, and ﴿asāwira﴾ with the tāʾ compensating for the yāʾ of ﴿asāwīr﴾. It was recited ﴿alqā ʿalayhi asworatan wa asāwir﴾ (with the verb in the active voice), with the agent being God, the Mighty and Majestic.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 43, verses 55–56:

﴿فَلَمَّا آسَفُونَا انتَقَمْنَا مِنْهُمْ فَأَغْرَقْنَاهُمْ أَجْمَعِينَ﴾ ﴿فَجَعَلْنَاهُمْ سَلَفًا وَمَثَلًا لِلْآخِرِينَ﴾

"Āsafūnā" is derived from asifa, asafan, meaning that his anger became intense. From it comes the hadith concerning sudden death: "It is a mercy for the believer and a seizing in anger for the disbeliever." [This was mentioned earlier in Ṭāhā.] Its meaning is: they went to excess in sins and overstepped their bounds, so they deserved that We hasten to them Our punishment and retribution, and that We not show forbearance toward them.

It is also read as salafan, the plural of sālif (like khādim and khadam). 

Salafan, with two damma vowels, is the plural of salīf, meaning a group that has passed on. Salafan is also the plural of salafah, meaning a company that has passed on.

Its meaning is: We made them a precedent (qudwah) for the later disbelievers, who follow them in deserving a punishment like theirs and its descending upon them, because of their committing similar deeds, and a wondrous account that travels like a proverb, which they relate, and it is said to them: "Your case is like the case of the people of Pharaoh."

**[Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on Surah 43, verses 66–73]**

*"That they come upon them"* (an-tatiyahum) is a substitute (badal) for *"the Hour"*. The meaning is: "Do they await anything but the coming of the Hour?"

If you say: does not His saying *"suddenly"* (baghtatan) convey the same meaning as His saying *"while they do not perceive"* (wa hum la yash'urun), so that one could dispense with it? I say: No, because the meaning of His saying, exalted is He, *"while they do not perceive"* is: while they are heedless, occupied with the affairs of their worldly life, like His saying, exalted is He, *"seizing them while they are disputing"* (ta'khudhuhum wa hum yakhissimun). It is also permissible that it comes upon them suddenly while they are alert (fatinun).

*"On that Day"* (yawma'idhin) is in the accusative, governed by *"enemies"* ('aduwwun), meaning: on that Day every friendship (khullah) between those who loved one another for other than the sake of God will be severed, and will turn into enmity and hatred, except the friendship of those who were friends for the sake of God, for it is the lasting friendship, which grows stronger when they see the reward of mutual love for the sake of God and mutual hatred for the sake of God.

It has been said that *"except the God-fearing"* (illa al-muttaqin) means: except those who avoid being friends with evil companions. It has also been said that it was revealed concerning Ubayy ibn Khalaf and 'Uqbah ibn Abi Mu'it.

*"O My servants"* (ya 'ibadi) is a quotation of what the God-fearing, who loved one another for the sake of God, will be called on that Day. *"Those who believed"* (alladhina amanu) is in the accusative position as an adjective (sifah) of *"My servants"*, since it is a vocative with a possessive suffix (munada mudaf). That is: those who affirmed Our signs and were *"Muslims"* (muslimin), sincerely devoting their faces to Us, making themselves wholly submissive to Our obedience.

It has been said: when God raises the people, everyone will be seized with terror, and a caller will call out "O My servants," whereupon all people will hope for it; then those who believed will follow it, and the people other than the Muslims will despair of it.

It was read *"O servants"* (ya 'ibad). *"You will be made joyful"* (tuhbarun): you will be made to rejoice with a joy whose effect (hibar) appears upon your faces, like His saying, exalted is He, *"You recognise in their faces the radiance of bliss"* (ta'rifu fi wujuhihim nadratan-na'im). Al-Zajjaj said: *"you will be honoured"* (tukramun) with an honour that is extravagant. *Al-hibrah* is exaggeration in describing something beautiful. *Al-kub* is a cup without a handle.

*"In them"* (wa fiha): the pronoun refers to Paradise. It was read *"tashtahi"* and *"tashtahihi"*. This is a restriction (hasr) of the kinds of blessings, since they are either desired in the hearts or delightful to the eyes.

*"That"* (tilka) is a reference to the Paradise mentioned. It is the subject (mubtada'), and *"the Garden"* (al-jannah) is the predicate (khabar). *"Which you have been made to inherit"* (allati uwrithtumuha) is an adjective of *"the Garden"*; or *"the Garden"* is an adjective of the subject, which is the demonstrative noun, and *"which you have been made to inherit"* is the predicate of the subject; or *"which you have been made to inherit"* is an adjective, and *"for what you used to do"* (bima kuntum ta'malun) is the predicate, the preposition being connected to an implied element, as in the adverbial phrases that function as predicates. In the first case, the preposition is connected to *"you have been made to inherit"*. It is likened, in its remaining for its people, to an inheritance that remains for the heirs. It was read *"wurrithtumuha"*.

*"From it"* (minha): the *min* is partitive, meaning you eat only some of it, while its fruits remain on its trees; so it is always adorned with fruit and laden with it. You never see a tree bare of its fruit as in this world.

From the Prophet ﷺ: "No man in Paradise will pluck a fruit from it except that there will grow in its place two like it."

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 43, verse 74–78:

﴿لا يُفَتَّرُ عَنْهُمْ﴾ means: it will not be lightened or diminished, from the expression of the Arabs: "fatarat ʿanhu al-ḥummā" (the fever subsided from him), when it calmed down from him a little and its heat decreased. And al-mublis (ﷺ) is the one in despair, silent with the silence of one who has lost hope of relief. From al-Ḍaḥḥāk: the criminal is placed in a coffin of fire, then it is sealed over him, and he remains in it eternally: he sees nothing and is seen by no one.

﴿هُمْ﴾ is a separator (faṣl, a pronoun separating subject and predicate) according to the Basrians, and a support (ʿimād, a supporting pronoun) according to the Kufans. And it has been read: ﴿وَهُمْ فِيهَا﴾, i.e., in the Fire. [[His saying "and it has been read: wa-hum fīhi, i.e., in the Fire" — perhaps the postponement of the discussion on this reading relative to the discussion of the preceding pronoun is an alteration by the copyist, because it contradicts the order of recitation. (Ṭ)]] And ʿAlī and Ibn Masʿūd, may Allah be pleased with them both, recited: ﴿يا مالِ﴾, with the kāf dropped for tarkhīm (apocope, shortening of a name in address), like the saying of the poet:

"Yuḥyī rufāt al-ʿiẓām al-bāliya... wa-l-ḥaqq yā māl ghayr mā tasif"

i.e., God will revive the crumbled bones while they are decayed. It is said: "rafatahu rafatan" when he crushed it to pieces. And rufāt is a noun from it, like fatāt. He said: the truth is other than what you describe, O Mālik; he apocopated it by dropping the kāf, as if he had informed them of someone's death and then his life appeared.

It was said to Ibn ʿAbbās: "Ibn Masʿūd recited: wa-nādaw yā māl." He said: "How preoccupied the people of the Fire are from tarkhīm!" [[I have not found it with a chain. In al-Bukhārī, from Yaʿlā ibn Umayya, that he heard the Prophet ﷺ recite it thus.]]

And from some of them: the beauty of the tarkhīm is that they cut off part of the name because of their weakness and the greatness of what they are in.

Abū al-Sarrār al-Ghanawī recited: "yā māl" with a raised vowel (rafʿ), as one says "yā ḥār" (O Ḥār). [[His saying "as one says yā ḥār" is in addressing Ḥārith. (Ṭ)]]

﴿لِيَقْضِ عَلَيْنا رَبُّكَ﴾ — from qaḍā ʿalayhi, when he finished him off. ﴿فَوَكَزَهُ مُوسى فَقَضى عَلَيْهِ﴾ (Moses struck him and finished him off). The meaning is: ask your Lord that He decree (an end) upon us.

If you say: how does He say ﴿وَنادَوْا يا مالِكُ﴾ after describing them with despair (ibsāl)? I say: those are lengthy periods and extended ages, so their states vary; they fall silent at times because despair has overcome them and they know there is no relief for them, and at times they cry out for help because of the intensity of what they suffer. ﴿ماكِثُونَ﴾ means: lingering. And in it is mockery. The intended meaning is: abiding eternally.

From Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both: He only answers them after a thousand years. [[Al-Ḥākim narrated it from the transmission of Sufyān from ʿAṭāʾ ibn al-Sāʾib from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding His saying ﴿وَنادَوْا يا مالِكُ﴾: he said: He remained with them a thousand years, then He says: "Indeed you are abiding." And al-Tirmidhī narrated from the transmission of Quṭba ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz from al-Aʿmash from Samura ibn ʿAṭiyya from Shahr ibn Ḥawshab from Umm al-Dardāʾ from Abū al-Dardāʾ who said: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Hunger will be cast upon the people of the Fire until it equals what they are in of torment, so they will cry for help. They will be given relief with food of ḍarīʿ (thorny plant) which neither fattens nor satisfies hunger" — the hadith. In it, al-Aʿmash said: "between his descending upon them and the answer of Mālik is a thousand years." And al-Tirmidhī said: Quṭba is trustworthy.

Some people of hadith used to raise this (to the Prophet ﷺ). This was narrated by al-Ṭabarānī and al-Bayhaqī in al-Shuʿab, and al-Ṭabarī narrated it from the transmission of Sharīk from al-Aʿmash as a statement of a companion (mawqūf) and did not separate the final statement. Then he narrated it through the route of Quṭba as a marfūʿ report, and did not do so either.]]

And from the Prophet ﷺ: "Hunger will be cast upon the people of the Fire until it equals what they are in of torment, and they will say: call upon Mālik, so they will call, 'O Mālik, let your Lord decree (an end) upon us.'" [[This is in the hadith preceding it.]]

﴿لَقَدْ جِئْناكُمْ بِالْحَقِّ﴾ is the speech of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, by the evidence of the reading of one who recited: ﴿لقد جئتكم﴾. When they asked Mālik to ask Allah Most High to decree (an end) upon them, Allah answered them with that: ﴿كارِهُونَ﴾ — you do not accept it, and you recoil from it and are repelled by it, because with falsehood comes ease, and with truth comes hardship.

Say: "If the Most Merciful had a son, then I would be the first to worship (him)."

Rendering the passage: "Say: If the Most Merciful had a son, and this were established and confirmed by a sound proof, a clear argument by which you could support it, then I am the first who would magnify that son and the quickest of you to obey him and submit to him," as one magnifies the son of a king out of reverence for his father. This is a statement given by way of supposition and illustration, for the purpose of exaggeration in negating the son and extending the refutation, so that the speaker leaves no doubt unrefuted, while at the same time expressing his own firmness in the matter of tawhid (affirmation of God's oneness). He has linked worship to the existence of a son, and that is impossible in itself, so what is linked to it is likewise impossible. Thus it takes the form of affirming existence and worship, while in meaning it negates both, in the most eloquent and forceful way.

A parallel to this is when a Mu'tazili (ʿAdlī) says to a Predestinarian (Mujbir) [Note: he means one of the Mu'tazila addressing one of the People of the Sunna; in this comparison there is considerable impropriety toward the Exalted, which is obvious. (ʿ)]: "If God the Exalted creates disbelief in hearts and punishes for it with everlasting punishment, then I am the first to say: He is a devil and not a god." The meaning of this statement, and what its wording and structure were made for, is the negation that God the Exalted creates disbelief, and His transcendence and sanctification above that, but by way of exaggeration in the manner we have mentioned, together with an indication of the ugliness of the doctrine and the error of its adherent, a definitive testimony to its impossibility, and a declaration of one's own disavowal of it and extreme aversion and revulsion from committing it.

Similar to this method is the saying of Saʿid ibn Jubayr (may God have mercy on him) to al-Hajjaj when the latter said to him: "By God, I will replace you in this world with a Fire that blazes!" He replied: "If I knew that this was in your power, I would not worship any god other than you."

People have strained to draw out of this noble, rich wording, full of subtle points and benefits, which independently establishes tawhid in its most eloquent aspects, several interpretations. It is said: "If the Most Merciful had a son in your claim, then I am the first of the monotheist worshippers of God, denying your saying that a son is attributed to Him." It is also said: "If the Most Merciful had a son in your claim, then I am the first of those who are too proud that He should have a son; from ʿabd (servant) comes ʿābid (worshipper): when one's pride is intense, he is ʿabd and ʿābid." Some have read it as: "al-ʿābidīn" (the worshippers).

It is also said that "in" is negating: meaning, "The Most Merciful did not have a son, so I am the first to say this, to worship and to affirm His oneness." It is reported that al-Nadr ibn al-Harith ibn Kalada... [text as given: "al-Nadr ibn ʿAbd al-Dar ibn Qusayy"] said: "The angels are daughters of God," and the verse was revealed. Al-Nadr said: "Do you not see that He has confirmed me?" Al-Walid ibn al-Mughira said to him: "He did not confirm you; rather He said: 'If the Most Merciful had no son, then I am the first of the monotheists of Makkah: that He has no son.'" It was also read as "walad" with a dammah on the waw.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 43, verses 86–87:

"And those whom they invoke besides Allah do not possess intercession, as they claimed that they are their intercessors with Allah. But [they possess intercession only for] one who bears witness to the truth, which is the Oneness of Allah, and who knows what he bears witness to with insight, certainty and sincerity."

﴿Except for one who bears witness to the truth﴾ [43:86]. It is an exception of the disconnected kind (istithna' munqati', i.e. the exception is not of the same category as what precedes it). It is also permissible for it to be a connected exception (istithna' muttasil), because the group of "those whom they invoke besides Allah" includes the angels.

It is recited ﴿تدعون﴾ (tad'un) with the letter ta' [in the second person], and ﴿تدّعون﴾ (tad-da'un) with a ta' and the doubling of the dal.

And as for His saying, "wa-qīlihi," it is read with all three vowel cases. Regarding the accusative, al-Akhfash mentioned that it is governed by an implied verb, as in: "Do they think that We do not hear their secret and their private talk?" and "wa-qīlihi" is also read as "wa-'anhu" (and about him) and "wa-qāla qīlihi" (and he said, "qīlihi"). Al-Zajjāj took it as a conjunction on the position (maḥall) of "al-sā'a" (the Hour), just as you say, "I am amazed at the striking of Zayd and 'Amr," and he took the genitive case as following the form (lafẓ) of "al-sā'a," and the nominative as a new sentence (ibtidā'), with the predicate being what follows. He also permitted its conjunction to "'ilm al-sā'a" (knowledge of the Hour) with an omitted noun (muḍāf) assumed: the meaning being, "With Him is the knowledge of the Hour and the knowledge of his saying." What they said is not strong in meaning, given that there is a separation between the conjunct and the conjoined by something that is not suitable as an interjection (i'tirāḍ), and given the disharmony of the composition (naẓm). Stronger and more correct than that is that the genitive and accusative are by the omission and elision of the particle of oath, and the nominative is according to their saying: "Ayman Allāh" (by the rights of God), "Amānat Allāh" (by the trust of God), "Yamīn Allāh" (by the oath of God), and "La'amruka" (by your life). His saying, "Indeed these are a people who do not believe," is the answer to the oath, as if it were said: "And He swore by his saying, O Lord, that indeed these are a people who do not believe." Or: "And his saying, O Lord, is My oath that indeed these are a people who do not believe." So "fa-iṣfaḥ 'anhum" means: turn away from their call, despairing of their belief, and bid them farewell and leave them. "Wa-qul lahum salām" means: "Peace," i.e., you are free from them, and a parting. "Fa-sawfa ya'lamūn" is a threat from God to them and a consolation to His Messenger (ﷺ). The pronoun in "wa-qīlihi" refers to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and God's swearing by his saying is an elevation of him and a magnification of his supplication and his appeal to Him.

From the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surah al-Zukhruf will be among those who will be told on the Day of Resurrection: 'O My servants, there is no fear upon you today, nor will you grieve. Enter Paradise without reckoning.'"
